utterances.text: In your defence, would you have been interested in evidence which tended to prove that you were not the person responsible even if it tended to identify who really was responsible?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I always asked that all the evidence be presented, both written evidence and eyewitnesses, particularly those two individuals. It was normal that the people in Prijedor knew everything about the event, because they were employed in the police force. Drljaca, Jankovic, all the head police people knew what their workers and members were doing. It was no explanation that they did not. This was confirmed by Mr. Vujin, later on in his contacts with Jankovic. He said that Jankovic told him the true story linked to the events. I heard many versions of the events but I always asked that they be checked. But since April 1998 onwards, Mr. Vujin and Mr. Livingston, because of the facts that Mr. Livingston had insisted upon, that is, to arrive at the facts, they came into collision, Mr. Vujin and Mr. Livingston. From April onwards, they didn't have any contact, so that I found myself in a very difficult situation, especially because Mr. Vujin insisted that he take over the investigation and look into the events in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, because that rather long answer was from a fairly short question by me, which is this: Were you interested in trying to get hold of evidence to disprove your conviction, even if it meant implicating other people in the crimes that you were accused of?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Livingston interested in pursuing that line?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What about Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He exclusively stuck to his own strategy, that everybody outside, especially those who had moved to live in Serbia, must not be brought into any kind of connection with the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you, at any stage, trial or appeal stage, want to run your defence on that basis? In other words, not wanting to implicate any third parties.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. Everything that I know through Mr. Livingston's investigation and the investigation led personally by my brother and the knowledge that he arrived at in the previous period, I conveyed that quite fairly to Mr. Livingston and Mr. Vujin to check whether it was true, and to see and to prove what was true, and to present the witnesses before this Tribunal, regardless of the consequences, regardless of who was in question, myself or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So help me about this. Page 6, near the top, back to the argument between you and Mr. Vujin on the 5th of September of '98, dealing with the incident with the two policemen, you say Vujin angrily replied that: "I was ungrateful, but he could not allow a new man to be indicted and particularly not a man from Serbia." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I absolutely stand by that. All the more so as that in the meantime I received information that he personally had helped many others to move to Serbia and to live there, so that these people were under control, were controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You go on to say that Mr. Vujin told you, during this argument, that he and everyone at the Prijedor police -- in the Prijedor police knew very well that Borovnica did not kill the two policemen that were dead and that that was the best solution. Again, do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I stand by that theory completely and what he told me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let me move on, please, to page 8. You've referred, in the statement, to a number of documents which you had come into possession of, and you deal, towards the bottom half of that page, with another discussion with Mr. Vujin where you say he repeated several times that he, as lead counsel, would decide what to submit and when to submit it. "He was completely clear when he told me that he would never allow any evidence to be submitted in my case that could jeopardise anyone who was at liberty in Yugoslavia or in Republika Srpska," and so it goes on warning you to be careful what you did because you had a family in Serbia and perhaps no one would be able to protect them. How did you take that warning, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I took that warning seriously. All the more so as all my former lawyers from abroad advised me that it was a good idea for my family to leave the territory of Republika Srpska, and that the greatest danger for their sojourn there were individuals who could be uncovered by the investigating organs in The Hague. All of them, for many years, for the most part, considered that once I was proclaimed guilty, they would all be free and that they could continue their lives as they had lived them hitherto. Apart from that, many of those people I knew were living both in Belgrade and Novi Sad, and that they had bought property there, and that they were in contact with people that had already been arrested here in Holland, and that they were well-informed about everything taking place in and around my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, just pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I want to ask him about his statements, but I would wish to ask him some questions relating to the material that Mr. Vujin has put in. It would appear that that's a natural break. I wonder, I see it's nearly 1.00. I don't know whether that might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I was looking at you inquiringly, Mr. Abell. It would help the bench if you would find it possible to indicate how much further time you might need to complete your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would hope - I would hope - to deal with it perhaps in half an hour. These things always are difficult. Please don't hold me to it to the minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One appreciates that very readily, Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then would it be convenient if we resumed at 2.30? The Court stands adjourned accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm going to turn in just a moment to the material which has been submitted in this matter by Mr. Vujin, but before I do, could I just ask you to do this: Obviously, listen very carefully to the questions I ask and try to just answer the questions that I ask. We all understand you want to say things, but listen to my questions and try to keep your answers short, if you can; all right? I'm sure that will help everyone. Now, first of all, I'm going to be looking at the documents sent in by Mr. Vujin dated the 19th of March headed "Submission of the Written Statements of Witnesses," and that bundle has the pagination on it 165, if that assists. Mr. Tadic, do you have a copy of that? You can be supplied with it if need be.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I would like a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm going to look at a statement at page 146, top right, of Djordje Lopicic, Dr. Djordje Lopicic. It goes from 139 to 146.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I've been given a text in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we may well be getting you one in your own language in just a moment. I've asked for that and it may be ready in a moment. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Good. Now, the first thing I want to ask you about Dr. Djordje Lopicic is this: Can you just help me as to what your understanding is of the relationship between Mr. Vujin and Dr. Djordje Lopicic? Is there any link between them?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And that is what, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: They have been friends for many years. I think that they are very close when it comes to Djordje Lopicic's stay in America as an ambassador and the education of Mr. Vujin's son abroad. So they have very close family ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: There is a statement from a (redacted) (redacted), is there not, in the bundle provided by Mr. Vujin. You don't need to turn to it just yet. Just answer "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know there is. I know there is a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: She is not, is she not, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And she is employed where?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: She is employed in Mr. Vujin's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, can you help me, please, on the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, would you give me the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, 145 on the top right. I hope I understand the pagination, Your Honours, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It seems to be in reverse order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It does, and I was a little curious about it. I hope that I have got it right. It's the second page. It begins with the words "Defence Counsel's," and it's 145 in the manuscript at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. You say that that is the statement of?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That is the statement of Djordje Lopicic. It begins at page 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, but you were talking of his daughter, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Only in passing, just to mention the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're not asserting that her statement is before us, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It is. It is further on in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: At what page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would Your Honours bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It is a little further on in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm looking now at page 145 of Dr. Djordje Lopicic's statement. He says that he discussed matters with you. Firstly, do you agree that there were occasions when you and the ambassador would speak?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: He says on that page, "I know for a fact that at that time Milan Vujin was very professionally, conscientiously, and expertly doing his work on the defence of Dusko Tadic." Do you accept that statement or not about the quality of Mr. Vujin's work on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: What I saw through my case, I thought it was not professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: How often would you discuss with the ambassador, Dr. Lopicic, the details of your case and the conduct of it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, the details from the defence case, we didn't discuss them much. It all boiled down to one in the same thing, the need to enable me to have an insight into all the written documents and the bringing in of the witnesses who were vital to my case. We didn't discuss any other details much, so the discussion was of a general nature mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: On your meetings with Dr. Lopicic, did you always discuss the details of your case or were there other topics that would be discussed?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: We discussed my physical state and quite different matters, questions that were not related to my case before this Tribunal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: On the same page lower down, about six or seven lines from the bottom, he says: "Mr. Vujin, on several occasions, visited the highest state authorities and personalities in the Republika Srpska." As far as you know, Mr. Tadic, when he did that, did he ever bring with him any foreign lawyer from the team, either Mr. Livingston or Mr. Wladimiroff, at the various stages, or Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He usually came alone. He did not like to contact the foreign lawyers much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm now on page 3, page 144 at the top, where Dr. Lopicic deals with his finding out that you had dispensed with the services of Mr. Vujin. It came as a great surprise to him, he says. He then says this: "The only thing that I mentioned to him was that it was not convenient that in his defence team there was not a single defence counsel, a Serb either from FRY or from the Republika Srpska." Do you agree that he just restricted himself to saying it was not convenient or did he say more than that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He said far more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Give us, please, the gist or a precis, just a summary of what he said to you when you decided to dispense with Mr. Vujin's services shortly before the trial.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about cooperation between the authorities of Yugoslavia, the Republika Srpska and the court in The Hague and the possibility of bringing witnesses to the Tribunal who would be defence witnesses, and he expressly said that I would get nobody if I -- it was in that context, that I shouldn't be stubborn because Yugoslav interests were at stake, far more important interests than my own and mine myself. So we had a much more lengthy conversation in that direction, and everything boiled down to the fact that my case was not only a case of me personally but that many more important things were at stake. He said that there was a case against Yugoslavia and a complaint from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when it was a case of an international armed conflict, that this could have a serious effect and that I must take care what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you were the man in the dock or about to be put in the dock on this trial. Who were you concerned with, your own position or the position of the state?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I was exclusively interested in my own defence and not anybody else's, especially not the defence of the state or important individuals who were at the head of that state. They all knew that very well. Everybody knew that, especially the foreign lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What impression did you get from what Dr. Lopicic was telling you in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Everything boiled down to the fact that unless I had people from Yugoslavia, that is to say, from Serbia, the Republika Srpska, on my defence team, that I wouldn't get defence witnesses, that I would not have access to material that could help my case. Quite obviously, this was held under the control of my defence team. Mr. Wladimiroff very often said that he wasn't interested in the defence of Yugoslavia and Serbia, that he was only working for my own interests. This very often irritated Ambassador Lopicic, and he would criticise me for that, reproach me for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, about two-thirds of the way down page 144, page 3, Dr. Lopicic says: "I most strongly refute the allegations that I was telling Tadic at the time that he would end up without a single important witness from either FRY or the Republika Srpska." Do you agree or disagree with that statement from this man?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with his statement. I think that it was quite the opposite. He raised his voice when talking to me, and he clearly let me know that I would end up as I have ended up. He made use of the people who knew me and contacted Mr. Lopicic, and they all came to visit me to tell me that I should listen to his advice. He even called my wife up for that purpose. He tried to exert influence on her, for her to tell me that I was making a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did she speak to you about that, your wife?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: From your conversation, how did she react? What was her impression of what was being said to her about getting you to change your mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: The whole time after I was arrested, I tried to keep my wife and children apart, because they had had a very difficult life and were finding it difficult. I was very sorry that anybody had asked her to use her influence with me. She was angry, and she said that she wouldn't have come to visit me in The Hague had she known they were going to do so. It was her first visit. She knew me very well and, of course, she knew that nobody could influence me, that I would do how I saw fit and how I thought that I should proceed. My wife and I have known each other since we were 15 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You say or, rather, I'm sorry, I draw your attention to the very bottom of that same page. "At the time Tadic was simply obsessed," is the word used, "with his Defence counsel Mr. Wladimiroff and his team." Do you agree that you were obsessed with them or were they simply your legal team?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I never had any dealings with a Court before, and the way in which Mr. Wladimiroff and his associates behaved towards me and my problem, the case that I was being tried for, was something that I was exceptionally satisfied with. There was no personal sentimentality of any kind. I was very satisfied with the professional relationship that they displayed and, quite simply, he didn't find it difficult to travel to Republika Srpska, and even the most remote village to check out some things, whereas other lawyers found it very difficult to go even 20 or 30 kilometres away and always found reasons why they should not go. But he did not find it a burden to go from Holland, or Steven Kay from London, for example, and that was something that I was extremely satisfied with, their approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So they would take the trouble to go out to your country and make investigations. Did they find it easy, though, to get hold of the people they were trying to get hold of?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult, and I was -- really marvelled at the courage they showed because, you know, in 1995 there was a war waging in the area, and I know that Mr. Wladimiroff spent some time in Prijedor when the territory was being bombed, in fact. There were also problems of entering the Republika Srpska from Yugoslavia, the acquisition of visas and so on. Everything was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: All right. I'm going through the page now, page 143, top right, he says this, this is Dr. Lopicic: "Tadic informed me by telephone that he had withdrawn his authorisation to Wladimiroff, and he wishes again to engage Milan Vujin." Firstly, the stage at which you decided to re-engage Mr. Vujin was after the trial -- after the evidence, but before the judgement; is that correct? Just putting it in context.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You have, to some extent, already dealt with this in your two statements that we dealt with this morning, but do you accept and agree with that statement by Dr. Lopicic, that you telephone him just to tell him you changed your mind? Did it come about like that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lopicic see you again before you changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He visited me, sometimes more frequently, sometimes less, but we always talked about the fact that I should include Mr. Vujin into the Defence team regardless of the stage at which my trial was at. He said that Mr. Vujin had exceptional relations with those people down there, and that he disposed of evidence which could significantly change the situation at the trial. Then I informed Mr. Wladimiroff of this and we discussed it at some length.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You've dealt really with the detail of that in your statement. I'm not going to ask you any more. So your case is that you were advised and told to hire Mr. Vujin again rather than your just telling Dr. Lopicic to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I was expressly given to understand that I would be able to -- that key witnesses would be brought and that Mr. Vujin had evidence in his hands, he had been in the field, and that it would be a great pity if I rejected this offer from him. I never made a secret of this. I discussed it quite openly with Mr. Wladimiroff, because it was in the interests of showing the truth before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, I think you saw, going further into the statement, page 140, page 7 you may have it as, Mr. Tadic, I'm sure, towards the end, he said the last time he saw you was on December the 18th of '98?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I haven't got that here but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you remember the occasion? Can you remember the conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think you saw Dr. Lopicic on the 18th of December, which he says was the last time you met him. Would that be right, the 18th of December last year?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: If that was during the visit of the Yugoslav delegation to the Hague, then my answer is yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He said he was in the delegation of the Yugoslav Federal Minister of Justice. Was there a conversation on that day between you and Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I talked to the head of the delegation, the Minister of Justice. I think his name was Knezevic, and Mr. Lopicic only partially took part in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In a nutshell, what were you saying to those people?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I told them -- I presented my impressions and knowledge linked to the work of Mr. Vujin and my Defence team. I particularly told them that some of the perpetrators of the crimes for which I was convicted were located in Yugoslavia. I even told them the addresses of those people and asked them to check them out, to check the exactitude of that information linked to those individuals. I told them quite openly that Yugoslavia was protecting the criminals that had escaped from the Republika Srpska. They didn't like hearing that. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: For a moment, Mr. Tadic, at whose expense, as far as you were concerned, were those individuals being protected?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, most of those people made a lot of money in an infamous way in the Republika Srpska, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: A misunderstanding perhaps in the translation. When I say "at whose expense," I mean who suffered by those people being protected, whoever was protecting them? Who was suffering?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: My own expense, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You say they didn't like it when you told them that. Can you remember anything significant that any of them said about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Knezevic, when I gave him some information, said, "Well, where do you get the idea that we're protecting someone from? If we are protecting them, then we're protecting the three officers that the International Tribunal is looking for." He told me that quite openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You mean to say he was accepting that some people were being protected?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting. "If I am protecting somebody, then I am protecting those three officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That's all I want to ask you about Dr. Lopicic's statement. Could we please go now to the statement of Zarko Nikolic, which is at page 135? I may be able to deal with this individual quite quickly with you, Mr. Tadic, whilst the statement is being obtained. He's counsel of a defendant Kos, Mr. Kos, and he speaks of accompanying Mr. Vujin to make some inquiries relating to what he calls the research centre at Omarska. Did, as far as you know, Mr. Vujin take any foreign lawyers with him on that visit?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. In that period, I remember that Mr. Vujin told me that they had made the decision that never again will anybody from abroad participate in the defence of any person from Republika Srpska, and that they would decide that amongst themselves, resolve that amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, did anything useful or helpful, from your point of view, emerge from that visit?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. These are just two statements of maybe some ten lines each but without any kind of relevant information, meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would you please be shown the statement of (redacted), at page 138, top right. Was he a legal assistant of Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I know that (redacted) was part of the Defence team, but the first time we saw each other, the first time we met was, I think, on September 4th in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm looking at the second or the middle paragraph in his short statement, when he speaks of that meeting. Did you ever see him apart from that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. We just exchanged -- Mr. Vujin introduced us, and I asked him how was it in the work, how was it going. He said, "I don't know. I'm just participating as a matter of form." So then I concluded that that man wasn't really doing anything. He even said he had come as a tourist. Then I told him, "Well, if it's like that then you don't need to come tomorrow or the next day." So for the next two days he didn't even turn up at all, even though the visit was scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So that we understand, was a visit to last three days. Mr. Vujin saw you on three days, but on the first day he brought this gentleman along, Mr. Kolesar, but not on the second or third day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he appear to have any real knowledge of your case?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, he said he had no idea. He said that he was only participating as a matter of form. So that's why I said there was no need for him to come at all. I had no use for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you say to him, is as suggested here, that you told him you were more than satisfied with the appeal and other work that Mr. Vujin was doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: We didn't really discuss my case at all. He had said he had no idea about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, can I please move on to the statement of (redacted) at page 134? Just to put her statement in context, (redacted) (redacted). Now, she suggests, towards the bottom of the first page of her statement, page 134, "All this time I personally contacted Mr. Dusko Tadic, who in each of our conversations told me he was very satisfied with the works of Mr. Vujin, and asked me to tell Mr. Vujin to do his best to get as much witnesses as possible from the investigating centre Omarska." Firstly, as far as -- firstly, do you agree that you did speak to her during the course of the time that Mr. Vujin was acting as your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. We probably spoke occasionally, but she conveyed messages to Mr. Vujin or from Mr. Vujin to me, so the topic of discussion that she mentioned never took place. This is the first time that she said that Mr. Vujin worked only on my case, which is absolutely untrue. I know that he also had some other five or ten cases alongside with mine. So he didn't exclusively deal with my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you take the opportunity on each and every occasion you spoke to say to her that you were very satisfied with the works of Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. No. She is the one who would sing Vujin's praises, saying he was a wonderful man. She would always give some attributes in connection with him and his work, saying that he had a good heart. Then she would always criticise Mr. Livingston, especially as far as the work on-site was concerned. She always said that Mr. Livingston -- it was his fault because Mr. Vujin could not develop his strategy. So she used to say that often, and then she would say that it was his fault that he couldn't do more for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you accept that or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I made no comments. I just felt that this was not true, but I was not in a position to enter into any kind of discussion with anybody, especially to talk about the policy regarding Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I ask you this: On the bottom line of that page, page 134, she uses the phrase, quoting as if they're your words, "investigating centre Omarska." Is that the phrase that you would have chosen to use yourself, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. I always used the term "camp." Only upon the insistence of Mr. Vujin and other Yugoslav attorneys we needed to make the correction into the "investigative centre." They would even correct text where it said -- if Mr. Livingston wrote the text he would use the term "camp," but this was then corrected by Mr. Vujin and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Tadic, we'll probably deal with that when (redacted) gives his evidence. If you'll just bear with me for a minute. If we could please go to page 108, the statement of a Mr. Slobodan Ivanovic, doctor from Belgrade. Firstly he says, towards the middle of that statement, that he visited you and examined you, but on that occasion you spoke about -- you spoke the best about attorney at law Milan Vujin, and about his professional skills, and his generous work and help that he gave to your family. Did you speak about Mr. Vujin to him? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: There was no mention. That man had nothing to do with the case. He was interested exclusively in the health of people, and especially connected to events related to the death of Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Dokmanovic. So I read that text. The majority of that text is absolutely untrue. What is true is what I wrote. He gave me a piece of paper, and I wrote down that he knows the readers of the Sunday Telegraph and that he likes painting. Because I wrote that, I began to receive copies of the Sunday Telegraph for free. That is all. It is true that he got in touch with my wife and that he promised her a job, but he never did manage to get her a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Are you referring now to what is near the top of his statement about his medical clinic Anlave?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Could we now go to the statement of Mr. Prodanovic? I'm just looking for the reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. I'm just trying to find the reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, this is the statement, 137, of (redacted), another attorney.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. (redacted). Forgive me. Would you please help me with this: Did you have a conversation with Mr. Prodanovic during the course of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did that conversation concern one of your brothers, Ljubo, I believe he's called, Ljubo Tadic, and does he live back in your country?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he lives in Banja Luka. The conversation was about the information that my brother Ljubo from Banja Luka provided which I tried to check through Mr. Prodanovic because he happened to be the lawyer of Mr. Kunarac from Foca. My brother had received information that there was somebody in Foca among the people who had taken part in the conflict in Kozarac, and they had told him that they were ready to discuss the events which could have an effect on my case because they were very familiar with my case. These were the people from the group of Sigara Danovic (phone) a well-known fighter from that area who were from Foca. I tried, through Mr. Prodanovic, to check whether these people were there in prison in Foca, and he sent me a message saying yes, that they were in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Pause for a moment, Mr. Tadic. If need be, you can go into a very lengthy explanation. Did you consider, from the information that you had, that these would be people that it would be very useful for one or more of your lawyers to interview with a view to obtain some evidence that might assist you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I believe that these were exceptionally important people, and I insisted that Mr. Livingston travel to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were those your instructions, that Mr. Livingston should go over there and try to hunt down this person and take a statement from him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. These people were there. I had received information, so it was just a matter of -- technically, it was a question of time for Mr. Livingston to go there and to take the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Livingston able to take the statements or did that not happen?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston left for Banja Luka with a day or two in delay, I'm not sure, but when he went to Banja Luka, I think that at that time Vujin had left hastily to Foca and had allegedly already taken the statement from that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Of course. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Abell. For the moment, we have a problem, the nature of which should become a little clearer later on, but for the moment, I think we can find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Really all I want to ask you is this, please: Mr. Livingston tried to contact this witness, wasn't able to. You say you believe Mr. Vujin had been there and had already taken a statement; did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was it helpful at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No, not at all, and I said right away that this was not the statement that I wanted, and I asked that Mr. Livingston take the statement. Later, he brought me a second statement, but before that, they returned that prisoner from Foca to Banja Luka. We took the statement from him; however, that was even worse than the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Who took the first and who took the second statement from this person?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin as well. He was not accessible for Mr. Livingston then. There was simply no way for him to meet with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The reason I ask you those questions is to come back to what I started on with this statement of Mr. Prodanovic. Did you and Mr. Prodanovic ever speak on this topic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Livingston's visit to Banja Luka, when he left with the intention of visiting the prisoner in Foca, and when all of that was over, I met Mr. Prodanovic in The Hague, in the detention unit, and that's when we discussed these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What did Mr. Prodanovic say to you about that episode?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: The problem was that Mr. Livingston had travelled to Banja Luka and he was expecting my brother to pick him up at the hotel and to take him to certain places so that he could interview witnesses, but my brother did not come to pick him up. Only when I spoke with Mr. Livingston, who said he was waiting at the hotel and he didn't know why my brother did not come to pick him up, I called my brother on the phone and asked him why didn't he go to pick up the attorney Livingston so that he could complete his work on the ground. Then he said that Mr. Prodanovic had called him on the phone --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: This is Ljubo, is it? This is Ljubo who told you this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that Prodanovic had told him not to go and pick up Mr. Livingston and to avoid any contacts with him, not to meet with him. He said that that was, in fact, a message from Mr. Vujin that he was conveying to him. I was surprised because of all of that. I know that I always insisted for him to contact and cooperate with all the attorneys working on my case, and then I told him to go to the hotel and to be available for Mr. Livingston and that it wasn't okay for this man to have given him this message. So I asked Mr. Prodanovic about all of this here in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let's pause. That's what I want to ask you. That's what I want to ask you. Did you put that suggestion, that information that you heard from your brother Ljubo, did you put it to Mr. Prodanovic when you met him in the U.N. detention centre here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What did Mr. Prodanovic say to you about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He laughed. He said, "Well, I just conveyed what Mr. Vujin told me to convey to your brother but I don't know what the background for that is," and I told him that it wasn't okay for him to interfere in my case and that he had made a mistake and not to do that again in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let's pause. Was he saying to you then that he agreed that he had rung up your brother Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that he had called my brother and told him not to meet Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Prodanovic tell you who had instructed him, Mr. Prodanovic, to ring up your brother and tell him not to pick up Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He told me that Mr. Vujin had told him that. So he had given him my brother's telephone number because Mr. Prodanovic had no way of getting my brother's telephone number. This is what Mr. Prodanovic told me in the detention unit, and he even apologised and told me that in the future he would not interfere in such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. That's all I want to ask you about the witnesses. Just wait there for a moment, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry that the time estimate was a little inaccurate. I apologise. I hope it won't be repeated. May I just indicate this: There are two other topics that I would ask about. Does Your Honour remember that this morning I said I took exception to the admissibility of certain matters? May I just explain briefly what they are? If we need to have a debate about that now, so be it. Firstly, Mr. Vujin has put in an article, a newspaper article from Slobodna Bosna, a newspaper, and I would object to the admissibility of that. Secondly, Mr. Vujin has put in on Friday of last week in English, late on Friday -- at about, I don't know, half past six English time I received it -- a file of correspondence between him and Mr. Tadic and vice versa. Again, I take exception to the admissibility of those documents on the grounds of relevance and, indeed, any questions of privilege would arise. I'm merely in Your Honours' hands. If it's going to be admissible, I would ask Mr. Tadic what he has to say about that now. If it's not to be admissible, I needn't ask any questions. If admissibility is decided against me later, then I would seek the leave to recall Mr. Tadic to deal with those matters. Alternatively, if admissibility is decided in my favour later, again, I needn't recall him to deal with those points. I'm merely in Your Honours' hands. I know that if those matters are admissible, Mr. Tadic has a diary which he's only been able to show me over the weekend, because it only became relevant over the weekend, in which he says he has put down his true thoughts about Mr. Vujin as and when events occurred which are consistent with the evidence he has been giving. I'm very much in Your Honours' hands as to whether I proceed to ask those questions now or leave it until we determine the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, I also have a dossier of papers presented by Mr. Vujin and which I have seen only latterly, but tell me, you speak of professional privilege as between Mr. Vujin and Mr. Tadic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Whose privilege is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It would, in my submission, be Mr. Tadic's privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He is before the Court and he is a kind of virtual complainant, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: He is a witness in relation to contempt proceedings. His evidence is important, of course, but his background sets for context within which the real allegations, those five allegations, are said to have occurred, and so his evidence is obviously important from that point of view, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can it be argued, I don't take a position on this, that Mr. Tadic by agreeing to testify has impliedly agreed to waive any privileges between him and his counsel, more so in view of the fact that his counsel is defending himself against certain allegations? How do you respond to that hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I look at the Rules in relation to privilege, and, of course, I understand the point about waiver privilege. I'm looking, if I may, at Rule 97 which is at page 74 of the 14th revision, the current Rules, and I see the way in which it is phrased there. It looks as if privilege, for the purposes of this Tribunal, Your Honours, is differently stated than perhaps we are used to in our own domestic legislation. I would submit if one applies that Rule: "All communications between lawyer and client shall be regarded as privileged, and consequently not subject to disclosure at trial, unless: (i) the client consents to such disclosure; or (ii) the client has voluntarily disclosed the content of the communication to a third party ..." It would be my situation that neither of those two situations has arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, suppose it is said that the word "consents" in Roman (i) should be construed in the context of the transactions of the day and that if the client is in the position of making or supporting allegations of professional misconduct against his counsel, he is to be understood as impliedly consenting to waive any privilege which might otherwise stand in the way. How do you react to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, I react to that in this way: Perhaps in our various domestic legislations, that might well be understood to be the case. One consents by or the client consents by the client's conduct, if I can put it that way, by giving evidence in this way. All I would say -- all I can say is that that is not what the words on the page say. It would mean a very wide and liberal construction, indeed, of that Rule to bring that about. That's the way that I would respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then shall we hear from your learned friends on the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: First the Prosecution and then Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution would agree with the interpretation which you just immediately proposed for two principal reasons: One, the actual applications thus far with regard to this matter clearly indicate that Mr. Tadic has been involved as a principal in bringing this complaint. The nature of his testimony, his assertions here today that Mr. Vujin was, in fact, obstructing his defence certainly only reinforces that point. Second, it should be considered that Mr. Tadic should not be able to use this device, in essence, a shield for protection, as a sword against his former attorney and at the same time deny Mr. Vujin his only possible avenue of defence in many instances by being able to withhold documents which might assist Mr. Vujin in his defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Mr. Vujin, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just briefly, I think that as a defence counsel dealing with criminal law for the past 30 years, I have very rarely been in the position of agreeing with the Prosecution. I would have nothing to add, however, to the position presented by the Prosecution. I think that we are on the same position, as is the Trial Chamber, that that is precisely the way of allowing me to defend myself from the construed allegations that have been made against me. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bench is in the pleasant position of agreeing both with the Prosecution and with Mr. Vujin, and that pleasure could be extended also to learned counsel for Mr. Tadic because although he took a point which counsel could take, I did not have the impression that he affixes great strength to his submissions. The submission is overruled. We have the reference to the newspapers. We're not quite clear about that, Mr. Abell. Would it be possible for you to proceed with your examination on the basis of our partial ruling, and perhaps when we return after the break, we would be in the position to resume consideration of that limb of your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is this the position, first of all, with the new bundle: Was the first time that you saw it yesterday afternoon when I came to see you in the U.N. detention centre?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did I bring with me the only copy that I had which was a copy in English?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did I give that to you to look at as best you could overnight?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And you handed it back to me this morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is this the position: Your only recent sighting of these letters has been in English and in a very hurried situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Nonetheless, do you feel in a position to deal with the matter in general terms?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can. There's no problem there --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: -- although I didn't understand 50 per cent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: There are in this bundle certain letters from you to Mr. Vujin which don't contain complaints from you to him; yes? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would you explain why you didn't, in writing, tend to express complaint about the way in which he was conducting himself on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, over a long period of time when I contacted Mr. Vujin, had contacts with him, I became convinced that criticisms of him and his conduct and work had no meaning. His household friend, Mr. Lopicic, and other friends that came to visit, such as Ivanovic and the rest, who knew him very well, they all prevailed upon me and said that the only useful thing for me to do was to give him compliments, and if I complimented him, his work would be better. I became convinced of this myself because I criticised him on several occasions over the phone, and he openly said that I wasn't to speak to him in that manner. Afterwards, I had no way of doing anything, except for trying to compliment him for what he had done and then to get more from him than I would otherwise have got and for him to do more than he did do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you ever put pen to paper and say in writing to him formally that you were, as it were, angry or dissatisfied with the way in which he was conducting your defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I think that the first and last time I did that was on the 28th of July, 1998 when I asked him to withdraw the motions he had presented to the Tribunal, that he was to inform Mr. Livingston of the contents of those motions and that afterwards we should decide together whether we were going to use that or not. However, I received a reply from him in which he refuses to withdraw the motions and in which he said to me that if I was dissatisfied, I should sever ties with him as counsel, and I have both those letters here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And is the position that they are in your language and they haven't been translated because we only saw this bundle of correspondence which has been relied upon by me on Friday evening and you on Sunday afternoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So that's a letter from you to him in July of '98 complaining about his submissions and the way he was putting things in your appeal?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I thought that it was natural for him to inform me of the contents of those submissions. I had no insight into what he was doing. Mr. Livingston didn't know what he was doing either, because he had no contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Livingston's doing or Mr. Vujin's doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin quite simply refused to contact Mr. Livingston and there were no contacts between them since April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What, if anything, was Mr. Vujin's reply to that letter?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I would just like to read out something briefly that is perhaps vital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is this in his letter to you or yours to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, would it be your intention to put in these two texts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was hoping to, yes. You appreciate it only just comes to light because of the way in which the bundle has been served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There is a way of doing it if you don't have translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, at such short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are they lengthy texts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I believe one is two pages and one is one page. The two-page one is in manuscript and quite close written but they're not lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, would it take a long time to get them translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I hope not, if the court can assist us to providing some translation overnight perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, what may be the position? (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. Abell, that translations could be made available in the course of tomorrow sometime, so what I suggest is that you may proceed with your examination on the basis of particular excerpts of the document, it being understood that the translated text will be available for tendering in evidence at some later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that, Your Honour. May I just mention that, on the same topic, I'm going to ask Mr. Tadic to refer to certain extracts from his diary. On the same basis may he refer to that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you have the only copy of the letter. You understand you're going to be asked to refer to the part to which you want to refer to on the basis that it will be handed over and an official translation will be prepared hopefully during the course of tomorrow. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The same will apply to your diary. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just read one sentence from the letter that I wrote to Mr. Vujin? I think that it is the crux of the matter. It is on the first page where it says -- I am addressing Mr. Vujin and say, "You independently and without my agreement and knowledge, in the past few days, submitted an answer to the complaint made by the Prosecution, and in the contents of the text and your intentions, nobody was informed, none the lawyers. Mr. Livingston was not informed either." So that would be the gist of the sentence and what was the important point. He responded by answering the following -- he says that he does not agree fully with the way in which attempts were being made of contacting the organs of the Republika Srpska. "I am informing you that I'm not going to withdraw a single line of what I, as the lead counsel, wrote and signed." Then in one other portion he says, "You are authorised as a -- as your lawyer that I can withdraw -- that you can withdraw your power of attorney to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You say that on the telephone you would have discussions from time to time about the way things were progressing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were they always conducted, if I can put it this way, quietly or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, I endeavoured to control myself. As far as criticisms, Mr. Vujin did not like any kind of criticism. If I were to criticise anything, he would say that he -- he would not allow me to talk to him in that way. That's what he would say. Then everything would end there. So I avoided criticising the work of Mr. Vujin in any way, and I considered that Mr. Livingston would be able to use anything that could be advantageous to my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, suppose we proceeded for another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I take the opportunity to ask, consideration might be given to the actual allegations made in the order of the Court. Perhaps you could bear that in mind in determining to what extent the testimony is really pertinent to those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I understand exactly. May I simply say this, that I feel that given that this material has been put in, Mr. Tadic needs to have an opportunity, albeit briefly and in general terms, to make his position on it clear. That's why I'm asking these questions about these documents, but I fully understand the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but you will understand there's another dimension of the matter as to whether or not certain evidence should have been pursued and should have been presented either before the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber. I rather think, though there may be a connection, the two things can be separated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can I ask you this, please -- just before we have the break, I'm going to ask you, please, to have a look at this diary. Would you? Now, I know that there are several references that you would wish to refer to. Can I ask you -- a number of them can be translated, but can I ask you specifically to look at certain pages? Firstly, before we do that, is this your diary?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: For what year is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I started writing it in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It has daily entries in it; does it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, not every day always. From time to time I write about the essential points. So I kept my diary at that time. In some places it is rather illegible, in other places better, but I read through the diary again because the diary was with Mr. Wladimiroff and I received it after a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You understand by referring to this diary it can be taken away and parts of it translated? You understand that; don't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And you wish to refer to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, although there are many entries there. I just made note of what I thought was important at this particular moment in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, don't worry. I'm certainly not going to ask you to recite to Their Honours the whole of 1996. Just, please, to give us the flavour. Would you please turn, for example, to page 35?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is that in February of '96?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, would it be your strategy to enter the diary in evidence? You're referring to a specific page. Are you relying on the diary itself for any evidential force?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The only force of the diary is that it is a memory refreshing document for him to assist this Court with what he says his true feelings were at the time. So I'm not introducing the diary as a piece of real evidence, but it is a means of his being able to refresh his memory as to what his true feelings were at the time. Also, of course, because he says he wrote it either on the day or within a few days of the date in the diary, it is evidence that that was what he was thinking, if the evidence is accepted, of course, subject to that. It is evidence that that is what this man was thinking at the date in the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You appreciate that your colleagues may have something to say on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I appreciate, but that's a matter for them, if they wish to make submissions. While I'm on my feet, may I indicate that my submission is that given that letters, correspondence between him and Mr. Vujin are in evidence, that he be entitled to show what he says his true feelings were about Mr. Vujin at the time which -- if I may just conclude the sentence, forgive me -- which he would say, as you have heard in his evidence, he chose to phrase himself carefully in his letters to Mr. Vujin, because he wanted Mr. Vujin, if possible, to give him results, and he felt flattery was the best option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I understand that. We will hear from your colleagues whenever they indicate a desire to be heard. I see Mr. Keegan on his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would, in fact, suggest that the complete diary should be submitted to the Appeals Chamber for its review of what information may be relevant in addition to the particular passages which Mr. Tadic would like to refer to. In addition, of course, we would like actual copies of the passages he does intend to refer to in his submissions, but we believe that the whole diary should be reviewed by the Appeals Chamber to determine what other entries may be relevant to this general matter, including the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're proposing that the diary in its original form be put in evidence or would a photocopy suffice?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would suggest, as a matter of practicality, Your Honour, that at the time that certainly it will have to be translated. Experience dictates that the Translation Unit will probably need the original to ensure that the photocopies are, in fact, of sufficient quality for them to be able to interpret before the document could be returned to Mr. Tadic, but our submission is that the entire document should be made available to the Chamber for its review. Both sides, Mr. Vujin and the Prosecution, should, at a minimum, be given copies of whatever particular sections that Mr. Tadic intends to refer to in his submissions during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But you visualise that translations would be necessary not in respect of the diary in its entirety but only of any particular parts which any party wishes to put in evidence; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again if I can only say from practical experience, that at some point perhaps a member of the Chamber would be assigned to review the entire document with somebody from the Translation Unit to determine what entries may be relevant in addition to those being referred to by Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm merely trying to abbreviate the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the diary as evidence, I am going to leave it up to the Trial Chamber to make a decision, and I shall accept any decision, because I am sure that I am not interested in any notes that the witness has made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, we propose a break at this point, and then we should be in a position to give you a decision on this point. So we will resume at quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, the ruling of the Chamber is it depends on the purpose, naturally, for which you have made reference to the diary. If the reference is purely for the purpose of refreshing the memory of the witness, then the diary need not be tendered in evidence and made available. If, however, you are relying on the document for its own evidential force, then another course will commend itself to us. So can you tell us very briefly what your position is? Are you just using this diary to refresh the memory of the witness as to the events to which he speaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It is a memory-refreshing document, in my submission. If I can put it in this way: Part of that, obviously, includes the date on which it was written, from which the witness refreshes his memory by looking at the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That is my submission of the status of this document. It's not a real piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. Then you may proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. There has been some discussion. The course I propose to take is to ask Mr. Tadic now, so that Your Honours have a flavour of some of the entries, I'm going to ask him to deal with three entries, but over the course of the next day or so a slightly larger selection, perhaps half a dozen or so, will be translated so the court can have that in due course, if that assists, a translation of what he has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, that makes me a little uneasy. You would be putting in the translations for their inherent evidential force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It's my mistake. Perhaps I didn't phrase myself properly. I understood the idea, I may have misunderstood it, would be that there would be some objective translation of what Mr. Tadic is going to refer to in the diary. I'm quite content that Mr. Tadic merely reads out those extracts, translating himself from his own language. I don't mean by saying that a written translation would be put in what I'm relying on is a piece of real evidence. Does Your Honour follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it your present proposal that Mr. Tadic should be reading out text of his diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: As a memory-refreshing document, yes. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, the position is this: Once the witness is going to read out the text of his diary to the Court, then the Court will be disposed to take the view that the witness is introducing those texts for their own evidential force. In those circumstances, the ruling of the Chamber will be this: The whole of the document will remain available to the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber, mindful of the peculiarities of the case, will itself go through the diary and determine whether there are any particular pages which should be translated. If it decides that those pages will be translated, they will be made available to the interested parties for such use as they may wish to make of it. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I don't know whether you yourself follow what has happened. I, on your behalf, am quite content if you merely look at your diary to remind yourself of what your feelings were on a particular day; do you understand me? If, however, you wish to read word for word entries in your diary, then the Appeals Chamber will take that as the whole diary being put in evidence, and it can be looked at by the Appeals Chamber, every single page of it if they wish. Now, I can do no further than explain to you what the situation is. If you use your diary simply as a prompter, as it were, to remind yourself what your feeling was on a particular day, that's one thing. If you choose to read out entries word for word from it, then the whole diary can be seen by other people. Do you understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: All right. I hope I have put it in layman's terms for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: For my part, but it's a matter for you, Mr. Tadic, for my part, I'm quite content if you use it as a memory-refreshing document. In other words, simply use it just to remind yourself what your feelings on a particular day were. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that I would like to quote some parts, and I don't have anything against anybody using the entire diary. I don't have anything to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic, but that is obviously a matter for you. I wanted you to understand, make sure that you understood the position before you committed yourself to that course; do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Would you look, for example, please at page 35 of your diary?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is there an entry there which relates to February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, February '96.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is there anything in that that you would wish to refer to first of all?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I wrote down what I was feeling at that time in relation to the relationships that were prevalent in that time in the preparation of my defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Will you help me, please? What is the date of the entry?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I said February '96. I don't think there is a specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: How soon after -- all right. So you would have written it when, in February of '96?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly but, yes, February 1996. I don't know the exact date. I would have to read the whole thing in order to find the exact date, but I would like to quote just one part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting: "Judging by things, it seems that Vujin has taken a partial role of Simic from Banja Luka formally participating in my defence but only to such an extent that my case does not cause broader consequences for the true participants in the events there from 1992, especially for somebody who is in Serbia at this time."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And "Simic" is a reference to whom?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: That's a lawyer from Banja Luka who, at the time of my arrest in the beginning, was participating -- was part of the defence team. That's a lawyer from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would you look now, please, at, for example, page 58?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is March of 1996, and it says in a part: "Vujin is convincing in every conversation, but the practice and the facts speak against him. It is my impression that he is part of my defence only in order to prevent the events from being uncovered relating to Omarska, and this is easiest for him to do by making it more difficult to investigate and by blocking the investigation, the questioning of witnesses, and the accused from Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: By referring to "blocking the investigation" and "the questioning of witnesses," whose investigation were you talking about and whose potential witnesses were you talking about, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the investigation which was being conducted at that time by Mr. Wladimiroff and his associates and I'm talking about potential witnesses that we had intended to use in my defence before the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In other words, blocking the investigation being conducted on your behalf by the other lawyers in your legal team, apart from Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "preventing the events from becoming uncovered," again, do you mean preventing the other members of your legal team, apart from Mr. Vujin, from uncovering the true facts to assist in your defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And that was March of '96; yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Written in or about March of '96 or in March of '96?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: In March '96. The month is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would you look, please, to two more references, perhaps? Page 64.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is text that I wrote in March as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: March of '96?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, March '96. I said: "By telephone, I spoke to Vujin, and he told me that a few days before he visited Bijeljina where he met with Minister Kijac. He did not go to Banja Luka and Prijedor which means that he lied to me again. I don't know how many times that is. I don't know the reasons why he did not go, but in any case, he says that he has obtained assurances that seven or eight guards from Omarska would testify in some way." Then further, I also state: "Vujin claims that a number of guards will testify for sure."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did any guards testify in the final event in the trial?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Finally, look at page 80.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The text was written in April 1996, and I wrote then: "Vujin is manipulating with my name, and he's coming out with a series of untruths, and he's making it known that all of my witnesses would be arrested in The Hague, even if these are ordinary civilians, ordinary people. This is a part of an interview that he gave to a Yugoslav newspaper."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Where did you get that information from, so that we're clear, that he was giving the story that any potential witnesses of yours or some potential witnesses of yours would be arrested if they came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: This was information from the newspaper, from an interview that he gave to a Yugoslav newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, that's by way of an example. I'm sure you have many, many other examples, but I hope, Mr. Tadic, that that's perhaps a reasonable representation of, can I put it this way, your misgivings during the first half of 1996 about Mr. Vujin's representation of you? Is that sufficient, as far as you're concerned, from your diary?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I would like to quote -- to read one more piece of text. It's something --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vujin (sic). I'm not going to prevent you. If you want to read one more, go on.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: It's something that's important. It's a text written in 1996 in which I state the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Could you give us the page number?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Page 79, side B, and I wrote --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I must intercede here. There has been a lapse. "Very well, Mr. Vujin. I'm not going to prevent you." It should state "Mr. Tadic" not "Mr. Vujin."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If I said "Mr. Vujin," I meant "Mr. Tadic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The correction has been accepted by Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I have not been making a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, go on. If I called you Mr. Vujin, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Page 79, in April 1996, I wrote down my remarks based on the information I got from Mr. Vujin, and the text goes: "I also informed Wladimiroff about the oral statement made to me by attorney Vujin as told to him by Zoran Zigic --" this is one of the accused "-- in connection with the events in the municipality of Prijedor. A) That for the first two months, he was the main warden of Keraterm. B) That he went to Omarska while he was drunk to beat prisoners together with Dusan Knezevic, Vlajic, Saponja and Kondic. C) That he was an intelligent man but that he did all of these things while he was drunk. D) That the story about not being in full control of his mind has been contrived for the purposes of defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
