utterances.text: Mr. Vujin told you that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'd like, please, to refer you just to one or two of the letters in the recently received bundle, the one you saw yesterday from Mr. Vujin, of correspondence. Would you look, please, at page 535?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I wonder if he could be supplied with the bundle.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't have it but perhaps I don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, if it's possible, I would rather you had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the letter? It's page 533 to page 535. It would be in the recent bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you have it now, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: This is a letter from you to Mr. Vujin dated July the 15th, 1997.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The original, no doubt, is hand-written?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We can see, just summarising it, that you refer to a meeting which had taken place with him in the detention unit in The Hague, and you were referring to a written text in relation to the appeal; is that right? In the second paragraph, you point out various mistakes and you list them.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You then, towards the bottom of the first page, say: "With no regard to the opinion of some members of the team for my defence, Mr. Livingston is a good and respectful lawyer and not a beginner." What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin always stressed that Mr. Livingston was young and inexperienced and that he was not up to this case, so that I wanted to tell him that he should not really be thinking in that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In your opinion -- I'm sorry. I cut you off then. Did you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I thought he was a valuable and an experienced attorney. At the beginning, of course, he didn't know my case very well, but later on when he was familiar with the case, I think he knew about it much more, and he knows more about the case than anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In your opinion, which of the two, Mr. Livingston or Mr. Vujin, was the most effective in getting at the heart of what a particular witness could say or could not say in your defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: The fact that Mr. Vujin maintained good links and had an exceptional position in Republika Srpska, Yugoslavia, and the municipality of Prijedor, that was a fact. But as far as the facts that were relevant to my defence, I don't know that he found any relevant facts by himself and that he presented any kind of crucial evidence with which he could help me before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, the Court allows considerable latitude to the parties, and we place our trust in you. There is, however, a relevance between this limb of your examination and the specific charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I put it this way: This bundle has been put in, no doubt, so that the comment can later be made, "Well, Mr. Tadic had no complaint about Mr. Vujin; he had a complaint about other counsel," and this letter and one more shorter letter are the only ones I'm going to refer to in any detail, and then I'm going to move on. In my submission, as this bundle has been put in, it is important to understand just one or two aspects of what Mr. Tadic felt about the way he was represented. I'm going to turn now, in fact, to page 3 of this letter and deal with the specific paragraph. I assure Your Honours that I have in mind what the five charges are, but as this bundle has gone in, it is my submission that Mr. Tadic must have an opportunity to say certain things about the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You wouldn't propose any faith in the ability of the Appeals Chamber to deal with this aspect in the course of your final submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I have every faith in Your Honours, of course. I just feel that my comment ought to be based, even just briefly, on some evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We wouldn't wish to give you the impression that we are, in any artificial way, endeavouring to limit the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I don't feel that at all. I'm very conscious of the fact that we must keep our eye on the ball here, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can I just come to the third page, page 533? You put in this letter, the paragraph beginning "because," "Because of all this and your personal role in the team for my defence, I suggest you not dissemble my intentions but disclose it all clearly in Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska and, also, your obligation to carry out my wish with no regard to your patriotic feelings for our common country and people." Why did you feel the need to write that sentence in a letter to Mr. Vujin in July of '97, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: This part relates to a concrete issue. It was about the fact whether it was necessary for my Defence to oppose the Prosecutor's demand whether there was an international conflict or not following after May 19th, 1992. It was thought that I should not really deal or oppose such demands, because I would not feel the consequences of any such decision. So that is what I stated here. As far as feelings, Vujin always stressed that it was important for him to represent the interests of the people that he belonged to, regardless of my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Finally on this bundle, I'm looking now at page 555, which is a letter from you to Mr. Livingston dated February of 1988 -- I'm so sorry, 15th of February of 1998. It is a letter which is critical of Mr. Livingston. What do you say about that letter?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember all the details, but the letter is the result of a series of misunderstandings that took place prior to it, that is say, prior to my contacting Mr. Livingston, because his engagement and involvement in my defence, up until April 1998, relations between him and Mr. Vujin were abnormal, in my opinion. They were not normal relations. I had occasion to attend joint meetings, and there were heated discussions during those meetings. So in some way, I was brought into a situation in which I had to take sides, to choose one lawyer above the other. I didn't really know what to do, what was the right course to pursue. So the letter is the product of the pressure exerted on me by Mr. Vujin and which he, on several occasions -- he on several occasions criticised me for Mr. Livingston's behaviour. Letters of that kind and telephone conversations, I sent many letters of that kind to Mr. Livingston, because I thought he would understand them as a positive criticism and that he would work better for having known them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, in terms of documents, the final thing I want to ask you about, if it's relevant, and I turn to Your Honours again, it's at page 167 of the bundle. It is a newspaper article, 166, 167, 165. The translation is at 165. I mentioned earlier that I challenged the relevance and admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The document headed "Slobodna Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed. Dated the 5th of December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have page 165 before me. It's the only page we seem to have here on the rostrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That is the only relevant page. The other pages would appear to be the foreign language, a photocopy of the article itself. That won't assist Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. The view of the Chamber -- yes, Mr. Abell, do help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's not page 169.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have it as 165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We have looked at 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If it assists in identifying it, it's contained in a bundle dated the 22nd of March of this year. That is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to the exact document which I have. This is entitled second line, "Slobodna Bosna newspaper of December 5, 1998, page 21."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The 165 here looks like 105.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If I may say so, I may sympathise. I have had similar problems. That's not being critical of anyone, of course, but I have had problems with the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bench has looked at this document and the bench is of the opinion that it is not admissible as it stands. If a formal document were to be presented, we might be able to review that decision. At the moment, the document as it stands is not admissible, so you need not prefer any examination to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I am very grateful to Your Honours for that, which means I have very nearly concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a few minutes after the half an hour that you indicated a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: For which I present, please, my profound apologies. Not intentional. I am perhaps not the best estimator of the time that the courts have ever known, I'm afraid. Please bear with me for one moment whilst I find the relevant part. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. In a document dated the 19th of March -- the bundle dated the 19th of March, Mr. Vujin makes a short statement. I'm looking at page 89 -- 88, 89, in which he states at page 2, and I can simply read it out, Mr. Tadic: "As always before, the interest of my client, therefore, the interest of Dusko Tadic was above and beyond everything, but up to the limit of establishing facts in connection with his indictment and establishing the truth in this respect." He is saying, Mr. Vujin, that his interest in you, his client, was above and beyond everything, and he wished to establish for truth in this respect. Do you accept or not that assertion made by Mr. Vujin, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You have said, in your statements and in your evidence, that he has been a party to obstructing your defence and the gathering of material that could be useful in your defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you know even to this day the extent to which that exercise occurred, how much your case was obstructed and at what stages? Do you know for sure?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I consider that it was exceptionally important and that Mr. Vujin, through his acts and the acts of his associates, contributed to the fact that this Tribunal did not gain a proper image of my role in the course of the war in 1992, and that because of that I was not able to present a series of other evidence which might have had an impact, might have influenced this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, that is all that I am going to ask you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, the diary would be made available to the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And the parties are entitled to inspect it. The court, in the meanwhile, will make its own arrangements to peruse the diary and will be providing copies of the relevant pages to the parties. In addition, the parties are free to inspect the diary if they so wish. Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you indicated earlier in your testimony that in response to the binding order, you gave instructions that only Mr. Livingston was to take witness statements. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that was so, then why is it that you asked Mr. Vujin to take the statements from Mr. Radic and Mr. Kvocka in April 1998 at the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I, first of all, insisted that this be done by Mr. Livingston, and every time when there were important witnesses, I always asked Livingston to take part. I did not wish to exclude Vujin either, but I had more confidence in Mr. Livingston doing it, except when it was not possible. Then I suggested that Mr. Vujin should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you indicating that Mr. Livingston refused to take those statements for you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Or is it that your position was simply being consistent with your letter of November 16, 1997, where you state that Mr. Livingston will question the witnesses, and I'm referring now to pages 536 of those documents: "Mr. Livingston questions the witnesses to whose statements he will refer in his part of the appeal, and Mr. Vujin should question all witnesses to whose statements we will refer in his part of the appeal."

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: That was partially correct. However, it was during a period in which Mr. Livingston and Mr. Vujin could not agree on working together. Then I remember very well they decided what part of the defence each one would undertake. This agreement, however, fell through later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your statement of 7 November, 1998, you state that you conveyed the message to Mr. Radic that you were following the instructions from Mr. Vujin in giving that statement. What exactly were those instructions?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I said that Radic, a few days before that, had publicly talked about me in front of everybody in the detention unit, and I discussed this with Mr. Vujin. Then, as I said, I asked him and Mr. Kvocka whether they would be willing to make written statements. When he agreed, I conveyed this to Mr. Vujin by telephone, and he suggested more or less what would be important for him to answer, to answer what questions. I mean, the questions that would be important to have an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Radic states that you, in fact, dictated the entire contents of that statement to him and he simply wrote down what you told him to put in the statement, although he says that other than the date and the references to Mr. Vujin, of course, that the information was true. Is that, in fact, what happened? Did you dictate the entire statement to him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. There was an intermediary. Another detainee intervened, because we did not have direct contacts. I would just enter his room from time to time. When he had finished, he handed it in via another detainee, Mr. Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, Mr. Radic states that the initial contact was initiated by you through Mr. Kunarac and that the statement was, in fact, taken in Mr. Kunarac's cell with you present, Mr. Radic present, and Mr. Kunarac present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: From time to time I did enter the cell, that is correct, but I did not dictate the text to him. I just read out the questions that my Defence counsel were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If Mr. Radic indicates that you, in fact, dictated that statement to him, he would be lying about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I think he was lying in that case, yes, because they were not the answers that I would have hoped to have got, and that is why I was dissatisfied and insisted Mr. Vujin come once again and take an expanded statement by Mr. Radic. I did expect a much more extensive statement and a more serious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Earlier you told the Judges that you had no idea why Mr. Vujin wanted the date of March 10 on the statement or why he wanted to indicate that he, in fact, took the statement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, your other counsel, Mr. Livingston, in his submissions, asserts that Mr. Tadic thinks that this latter suggestion, that is, in reference to the date of 10 March, may have been made so as to avoid any suspicion of Mr. Tadic having contact with Mr. Radic. Would that, in fact, be an accurate statement of why the date was fabricated?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: That is the opinion of Mr. Livingston. I can only suppose, but I really don't know. I personally think that it was a period when Mr. Vujin was in Prijedor, and probably whether he had proof that he was there or not, I don't know, but I think that around that date he did go to Prijedor. Later on I thought about that date, and I think that that is what it was about and not anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also stated, and you just referred to it again here earlier, that in addition to Mr. Radic, you also approached the accused, Kvocka, to give a similar statement but that he, in fact, refused you. You stated --

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You stated that when he -- he refused to give you a statement unless Mr. Vujin took it, that thereafter you called Mr. Vujin and he, in fact, came to The Hague and took a statement from both Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that was the case, then why was it that Mr. Vujin refused to come to take the first statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't say that he expressly refused. He said that he had no time at that particular moment and that everything was under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So you endeavoured yourself to take that statement from Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Vujin told me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You knew that the date placed on that first statement, March 10th, was incorrect; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I didn't think about that. Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So too did Mr. Radic know that that date was a lie; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: He probably did know. He was at liberty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also knew that the information in that statement, wherein it referred to the fact that it was being given to Mr. Vujin, was also a lie; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I proceeded according to what Mr. Vujin had told me, and he told me that that was not my problem. Apart from that, I said that I was dissatisfied and that I insisted that he come again and take an extensive statement. I did not insist that that statement be sent to the Tribunal because I personally was dissatisfied with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Radic also knew that that information, that is relating to it being given to Mr. Vujin, was a lie as well; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I can only suppose that it is. I don't want to enter into the text, but as far as the date and place are concerned, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You then submitted that statement to your counsel so that he could submit it to this Tribunal; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I submitted it to Mr. Vujin, and I did not insist that it be further submitted, but I insisted that he take an extensive statement, an expanded statement, and the statement given to me by Radic didn't represent anything very important, in my assessment, particularly with respect to the events that took place in the hangar, and that is what I had the most objection to in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, it's your testimony that Mr. Radic, in his explanation about the taking of that statement to members of this Tribunal, is also a lie?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he said, what he said as to the statement, but the statement was given to me in the U.N. detention unit. He gave it to me personally, and I proceeded, according to the instructions of my lawyer from Yugoslavia, without knowing the way in which he would use that and how he would use that, whether as a basis for further investigation or whatever but, in any case, I was dissatisfied with the statement. I expected a more expansive statement about the events, and I thought that he could testify about the events in Omarska camp, in particular, and the hangar of the Omarska camp, and I said this to Vujin. But in the second statement, once again, the hangar is just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Radic wasn't willing to give you that information directly either, was he?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Radic said that quite openly. He talked about the events in Omarska quite openly but always said that he did not know who the second participant in the events was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Speaking of additional statements submitted, let's move to the statement by Zoran Zigic, and the statement by (redacted), submitted in November -- excuse me, October of this year. He states that -- that would be the statement dated 29 October, 1998, and the reference is on page 5307 of the record, Your Honour. (redacted) states that, "Vujin also told me that Zigic would give a statement that he took Amir Karabasic, Jasko Hrnic, Alic, and Harambasic to Keraterm and Vujin and all of us knew that that statement was not true." (redacted), of course, also told you this, did he not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: No. The information that you are talking about I heard for the first time personally from Mr. Zigic in the detention unit, because he maintained that he was my principle witness and I maintained that he was not. That is why we quarrelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So the state of the evidence then is this,

utterances.speaker: MR. TADIC
utterances.text: Your counsel, Mr. Vujin, has submitted two statements, one that you know has information which was a lie on it, and a second one that your brother asserts has information that's a lie on it. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: As far as the statement of Mr. Radic goes, I cannot say what he wanted to say by giving his answers, whether he gave them honestly or not. I can't say anything as to the exactness of those statements. I just say that I was not personally satisfied with the answers. As far as Mr. Zigic is concerned, I personally consider that after talking to Zigic, when he came to The Hague, that he was used by Mr. Vujin to defend somebody else, because what he testified in his statement did not influence my defence at all. You know full well what I was accused of, and this had nothing to do with the testimony that Zigic made, but it was an occasion to defend somebody else, to prove that there were no dead people in Omarska. That was the defence priority of all the people in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, these conversations you had with Mr. Zigic, you had these conversations at the same time that you were under an order prohibiting contact between you and Mr. Zigic in the detention unit; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: True. However, Zigic did not sleep on our floor, and he is a man who entered my cell and, in that way, addressed me, and I said that to Mr. McFaden in a letter to Mr. McFaden in December 1998 and explained the manner in which contact between us occurred and asked him to prevent it from happening, after which he was transferred to the third floor, because these conversations with Mr. Zigic were far from pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you indicated in your testimony that Mr. Vujin told you, in part, that he would never jeopardise any individual who had his liberty in Yugoslavia or in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that statement is true, how do you explain the filing submitted by Mr. Vujin on your behalf in January and February and May of 1998 in which he extensively refers to others who allegedly committed the crimes of which you were convicted, including approximately six different individuals who apparently look like you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: It was at my insistence. I insisted that the truth be brought to the light of day, but you could note that Mr. Vujin never names anybody who is at liberty or who is alive. It was usually individuals either who were dead or who had been arrested, the individuals that he mentions in his statements, or even if he does quote some individuals, he does not say where they reside but gives a different place of residence. For example, he took some statements in Belgrade, whereas he states that the statements were taken in Prijedor to keep their place of residence confidential. Mr. Jankovic gave the statement in Prijedor but he said that the statement was made in Budapest, and that was the practice that Mr. Vujin resorted to. I asked him about this practice, and he explained to me that this was through the express demand of those particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also referred to a woman who Mr. Vujin said he would never allow to testify; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Again, do you have any explanation for why then that woman is clearly identified in the submissions filed by Mr. Vujin on your behalf in which he refers to her evidence relating to the commission of the crimes of which you were convicted by others?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: It was a generally known part of the testimony which the Court, the regular Court, that is to say, the first defence did not consider to be honest and sincere. Mr. Wladimiroff contacted the woman and he had this information, and Mr. Livingston was the only one who learned something new from the woman. But Vujin was against having that particular testimony, which represented a new element, to be presented before this Tribunal, and her testimony linked to Omarska was a generally known fact, and he agreed to it for that reason because it did not bring any fresh elements to light, but what Mr. Livingston detected was a fresh element.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did Mr. Livingston bring that information forward?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: You know that that woman asked for protective measures for her to be able to talk about key facts before this Tribunal, and she asked for protective measures because after contact with Mr. Livingston -- you must know one thing, that Mr. Livingston arrived at key information through his meeting with that woman and Miroslav Tadic. He had the meeting with the woman secretly. He was cautioned and invited by the police for investigation. You know that she was threatened and her first husband was killed at Omarska. As I say, her husband was in prison in Belgrade, and Vujin helped set him free, and in that way, he was able to control that woman. She had agreed to go to testify to the key events in Kozarac only if she was assigned protective measures to come to The Hague and not to return to Omarska anymore, because she thought that she would be subjected to maltreatment if she returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The relevance of whether she was granted protective measures, since her evidence was not accepted, the point is the information that she had was brought forward to this Appeals Chamber by one of your counsel; is that not, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, this is again a procedure upon which Mr. Vujin insisted. I was in such a position, and I've already said that from April 1998, Mr. Livingston and Mr. Vujin did not have any contacts. All of their contacts went exclusively through me, so I was in the position of accommodating either one or the other. Vujin always insisted that all the exchange of papers and everything always goes through him, and he was right because he was the counsel in chief. Mr. Livingston insisted he would ask me to make requests to Mr. Vujin. So in a way, this is how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just a few minutes ago, you indicated that, in fact, Mr. Vujin did submit the submissions in accordance with your directions; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't know which submissions you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When I asked you the question regarding the submissions filed by Mr. Vujin on your behalf in January, February, and May of 1998 and asked you to reconcile the information contained therein in comparison with the allegations you've made, you indicated that Mr. Vujin had filed those submissions, had included that information regarding these supposed others who committed offences at your direction.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I was not involved directly in those things. The only thing that I was interested in in principle was what Mr. Livingston insisted on, and I tried to help him in order to obtain new facts. At no point in time did I see, in anything that Vujin presented and what he tried to present to me, that this represented any new fact. I always consulted with Mr. Livingston about each one of those things, and I simply was not in the position to assess what was useful and what was not. I couldn't. I didn't particularly insist on what should be submitted. I just insisted on the things that should not be submitted. This was regarding the motion responding to the request of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Earlier, you testified to questions from Mr. Abell that your wife, in fact, knew that no one could influence you and that you would do how and what you saw fit and how things would proceed in your defence; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't think that she knew much about the manner of my defence. This referred to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether she knew about your defence. I'm asking if she knew about you and your character.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: She knows my character, that I am a man who tried to make decisions independently without anybody's influence. But in the position that I was in for more than five years, very frequently, I was not in the position to be able to evaluate what was good or what was bad for my defence. So I generally consulted with my lawyers or other lawyers, and these were mostly people from abroad about whom I believed that they were independent, who could give me useful advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would like to turn now just briefly to these letters which you sent to your counsel which, on

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: letters to Mr. Vujin that were only complimentary because that was the only way you felt that his work would improve; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let's look at some of these complimentary letters. I begin with the first letter, which is dated March 4, 1997. That would be pages 556 and 557. Looking at the second paragraph, the third full sentence in the translation -- well, first let's talk about the first sentence. The translation indicates you said: "First of all, I have to tell you that a few weeks ago I got in touch with the high persons in Republika Srpska. I did it in a direct or indirect way and at the same time had consultations with Mr. Wladimiroff." The translation goes on to say: "Mr. Wladimiroff knows me very well, and he does not try to make any influence on my future intentions regarding my defence. I mention this to make you understand that I am, after three years, capable and ready to take my decisions by myself and based only on my experience and well valuation." I presume that's "evaluation." You go on to say: "I do not have any questions in that regard and am ready for drastic changes. It is a question of a strategy, reasons, and in that regard, there is no place for my sentimentality where everything is directed towards my struggle for my bare life." By that language, were you intending to pay him a compliment or were you giving Mr. Vujin directions?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I do not recall how I felt at that time. In any case, I don't think that there's any compliment here. I think it was just a matter of exchanging information. I don't think that I was always paying him compliments. I had more important things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let's just go to the second page of that same letter. It's a continuation of a paragraph from the prior page, and it begins at the end of the seventh line: "I am interested only in new evidence, papers, and witnesses. Because of all this, I want you to be active in the further work on the preparation for the appeal before the higher Chamber and particularly in the request concerning new evidence." Again, were you intending to give him directions on how to proceed in your defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO TADIC
utterances.text: I was purely letting him know. I was expressing my opinion, what was important, in my opinion, to continue the proceedings in my defence, particularly in light of the consultations that I often had with other attorneys from abroad about what would be good and what would not be good. Of course, I was not able to then, and I'm still not able today, to evaluate facts, what this Court believes are facts. I cannot claim to be able to know what a true fact is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- it's coming up to 5.30. Would you like to indicate how much longer you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Given the prior experience this afternoon, Your Honour, I would be a little reluctant to peg a specific time, since I can't always account for how long the potential answers may be, but I would suggest that I should be able to conclude within an hour tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you're not erring on the side of generosity, are you? May I suggest, without wishing to curtail the proceedings in any way, that we might try to make the most efficient use of the resources of the Chamber and of the available time by interrogating ourselves on the question of how really relevant some of the material is to the five specific allegations which have been made? As you go through your field of inquiry, perhaps you might like to ask yourself, "How does this bear upon one of these five allegations?" I do understand that relevance is not always to be judged by reference to how directly it impacts on the issue, but on the other hand, there can be a question of taking the view that some material, is only peripherally or subliminally of relevance to those issues. Perhaps you could consider that overnight as we take the adjournment now until 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
